```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(pollinatoR)
```

## The design

Field studies of crop pollination often work in commercial paddocks rather
than on a trial site. In each field, a caged quadrat is matched with a nearby
open quadrat, and several plants are harvested from each. Fields differ in
soil, sowing date and management, so the comparison is read within each field,
where those differences cancel.

The data below are simulated with the shape of such a study in canola: 24
fields in three regions, one caged and one open quadrat per field, five plants
per quadrat. Honey bee visits are counted on each open-quadrat plant. Two yield
components are recorded per plant: pod count and seed weight.

```{r data}
set.seed(31)
n_field <- 24L
n_plant <- 5L
fields <- sprintf("F%02d", seq_len(n_field))
fertility <- setNames(rnorm(n_field, 0, 0.25), fields)
region <- setNames(rep(c("North", "Central", "South"), each = 8L), fields)

study <- expand.grid(
  plant = seq_len(n_plant),
  trt = c("Caged", "Open"),
  field = fields,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
study$region <- region[study$field]
f <- fertility[study$field]
open <- study$trt == "Open"

# Busier fields are also more fertile; visits do not change yield within a field
study$visits <- ifelse(open, rpois(nrow(study), exp(1.5 + 1.2 * f)), 0)
pod_mu <- 120 * exp(f) * ifelse(open, 1, 0.8)
seed_mu <- 6 * exp(f) * ifelse(open, 1, 0.85)
study$pods <- rnbinom(nrow(study), mu = pod_mu, size = 25)
study$seed_g <- rgamma(nrow(study), shape = 20, rate = 20 / seed_mu)
study$rainfall <- round(300 + 200 * f)
study$veg_biomass <- round(rgamma(nrow(study), shape = 15, rate = 15 / (90 * exp(f))), 1)
head(study)
```

Pollinator access was planted to add 25% to pod count over the caged plants
(a loss share of $1 - 0.8 = 0.20$) and about 18% to seed weight (a loss share of
0.15).

## Data, design and estimand

Each field is one matched pair. In a `matched_pairs` layout the pair carries a
random intercept, and the design warns if any pair lacks an arm.

```{r declare}
pd <- pollin_data(
  study,
  response = c("pods", "seed_g"),
  treatment = "trt",
  unit = "field",
  groups = "region",
  exposures = "visits",
  adjust = "rainfall"
)
pd
ds <- pollin_design(
  pd,
  arms = c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"),
  layout = "matched_pairs"
)
ds
```

The dependence compares caged plants with open ones. The assumptions for this
layout include one that a randomised plot trial does not need: the two
quadrats in a field must be alike apart from the cage.

```{r assumptions}
est_loss <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "loss")
knitr::kable(pollin_assumptions(est_loss))
```

## Loss share and gain, side by side

A loss share answers "what part of the yield now harvested do pollinators
supply?". A gain answers "how much would a pollinator-free crop rise if they
returned?". For an economic valuation of pollination the loss share is the
right number. Both come from the same pair of expected values, so the gain is
always the larger of the two: with a loss share $D$, the gain is $D/(1 - D)$.

```{r basis}
est_gain <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "dependence", scale = "ratio", basis = "gain")
loss <- pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_loss))
gain <- pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est_gain))
loss
rbind(loss$table, gain$table)[, c("response", "basis", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

Each response gets its own model and family: a negative binomial for the pod
counts and a Gamma with a log link for seed weight, chosen from the values.

## Further scales

The difference scale keeps the response's units (pods per plant, grams per
plant), which is what a yield budget needs. The RII and the log response ratio
are the scales most often used to compare studies.

```{r scales}
scale_rows <- lapply(c("difference", "rii", "lnrr"), function(s) {
  est <- pollin_estimand(ds, family = "dependence", scale = s, basis = "loss")
  pollin_effects(pollin_fit(est))$table
})
do.call(rbind, scale_rows)[, c("response", "scale", "estimate", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

For comparison with earlier work, `pollin_index()` gives the descriptive
indices from the field-level arm means, with intervals.

```{r index}
pollin_index(ds, response = "pods", n_boot = 500, seed = 1)
```

## From the sampled fields to the growing area

The 24 fields are eight per region, but the regions grow different areas of
canola. Suppose the North grows 2,000 ha, the Central region 1,000 ha and the
South 500 ha. `pollin_population()` declares the regions as strata weighted
by area. The model is fitted with the region as `by`, and `pollin_draws()`
returns the loss share per region and for the population.

```{r population}
regions <- pollin_population(
  "region",
  c(North = 2000, Central = 1000, South = 500),
  label = "canola area by region"
)
est_pop <- pollin_estimand(ds, "dependence", "ratio", "loss", population = regions)
dr <- pollin_draws(
  pollin_fit(est_pop, by = "region"),
  n = 1000L,
  response = "seed_g",
  seed = 1L
)
summary(dr)[, c("level", "median", "conf.low", "conf.high")]
```

The population loss share is $1 - \sum w\,\mathrm{caged} / \sum w\,\mathrm{open}$,
a ratio of the area-weighted arm means. It is not the area-weighted mean of
the regional loss shares, shown below for comparison.

```{r weighted-mean}
w <- regions$weights
weighted_mean <- dr$estimate[, names(w)] %*% w
quantile(weighted_mean, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))
```

The ratio of means weights each region by its area times its open yield,
that is, by its share of the seed harvested. A loss share is a share of
harvested seed, so that is the weighting it needs.
In these estimates the North yields most and loses least, so the weighted
mean of the regional shares comes out higher. (The regions were simulated
with the same loss share; their estimates differ by chance.) The gap widens
as regions differ more in yield and in dependence.

## Guard: a between-field slope is not a plant-level effect

The fields with more honey bee visits also yield more. Read across fields, that
looks like a pollinator effect on yield. In these data it is not: the busier
fields are the more fertile ones, and within a field the plants with more visits
yield no more than the others. `pollin_guard_ecological()` splits the exposure
into its between-field and within-field parts and warns when only the
between-field slope is distinguishable from zero.

```{r ecological}
open_plants <- study[study$trt == "Open", ]
pollin_guard_ecological(
  open_plants,
  exposure = "visits",
  response = "pods",
  unit = "field"
)
```

## Guard: adjusting for a downstream covariate

A cage does not change the rainfall a field receives, so adjusting for rainfall
is safe. Vegetative
biomass is different: plants that set fewer pods may put more into leaves and
stems, so biomass sits downstream of the treatment. Adjusting for it would
remove part of the pollination effect from the contrast. Whether a variable is
downstream is a judgement about the crop that the data cannot settle, so
`pollin_guard_posttreatment()` takes it as a declaration and checks the
declared adjustment covariates against it.

```{r posttreatment}
pollin_guard_posttreatment(pd, downstream = "veg_biomass")

pd_bad <- pollin_data(
  study,
  response = c("pods", "seed_g"),
  treatment = "trt",
  unit = "field",
  adjust = c("rainfall", "veg_biomass")
)
try(pollin_guard_posttreatment(pd_bad, downstream = "veg_biomass"))
```

The first call returns silently because rainfall is not declared downstream.
The second stops before any analysis uses the biomass adjustment.

The same judgement can be written as a causal graph. With the `dagitty`
package installed, `pollin_dag()` reads the graph, works out which columns are
downstream of the cage, and the guard takes them from it:

```{r posttreatment-dag, eval = requireNamespace("dagitty", quietly = TRUE)}
pd_both <- pollin_data(
  study,
  response = c("pods", "seed_g"),
  treatment = "trt",
  unit = "field",
  adjust = c("rainfall", "veg_biomass")
)
ds_both <- pollin_design(pd_both, c(excluded = "Caged", open = "Open"), "matched_pairs")
g <- pollin_dag(
  ds_both,
  "dag { trt -> veg_biomass -> yield; trt -> yield; rainfall -> yield }",
  "yield"
)
try(pollin_guard_posttreatment(ds_both, dag = g))
```

When the question is the direct effect of pollination with biomass held
fixed, the estimand asks for it by name (`effect = "direct"`) and the guard
lets the mediator through; *Identification in a field study* works through
both readings.
